section_1.title: Introduction: Setting the Challenge
section_1.content: Introduce the problem: Given two points A and B (with B lower and to the right of A), find the path a particle must follow under gravity to travel from A to B in the shortest time. Contrast this with the straight line (the shortest distance).
section_1.example: Visual animation showing a marble rolling down a straight line, a deep arc, and a shallow arc, where the middle path wins.

section_2.title: Prerequisite Intuition: Kinetic vs. Potential Energy
section_2.content: Briefly review the Law of Conservation of Energy. Explain that a steeper initial descent builds up speed (kinetic energy) faster, which is the key 'trade-off' strategy to solve the problem.
section_2.example: Visualizing a roller coaster: High potential energy at the start converts into velocity, allowing the object to traverse the later, flatter sections of the track much faster.

section_3.title: The Geometry of the Solution: The Cycloid
section_3.content: Introduce the Brachistochrone curve: the Cycloid. Explain it as the path traced by a point on the rim of a rolling circle. Show how its curvature optimally balances 'gaining speed' with 'shortening the distance'.
section_3.example: An animation showing a wheel rolling along a horizontal line; a red dot on the rim traces the exact shape of the optimal path.

section_4.title: Conceptual Proof: Snell’s Law Analogy
section_4.content: Explain that light follows the path of least time (Fermat's Principle). By analogy, gravity acts like a medium with a variable refractive index where the speed increases as the particle goes deeper.
section_4.example: Showing light bending through layers of glass with different densities compared to a particle accelerating through a gravitational gradient.

section_5.title: Conclusion & Real-World Significance
section_5.content: Summarize that the shortest distance is not always the fastest time. Mention the Calculus of Variations as the mathematical tool used to derive this formally, and its application in modern engineering (e.g., chute design, transit systems).
section_5.example: An animation of a slide design: Comparing a 'straight' slide vs. a 'cycloidal' slide to show why the latter feels like a 'rush' at the start and finishes faster.
